title: Module 5 assessment
subtitle: Lookup & Reference Functions
description: Fifteen questions across the whole of Module 5. Every question explains its answer, right or wrong.

questions.question: `=VLOOKUP(A2,Data!B:F,3,FALSE)` returns a value from which column?
questions.explanation: The column index counts from the first column of the lookup range, not from column A of the sheet. B is 1, C is 2, D is 3. Counting from the sheet instead of the range is the classic VLOOKUP error.

questions.question: Leaving VLOOKUP's fourth argument out gives an exact match.
questions.explanation: Omitting it gives TRUE - approximate match - which on unsorted data returns confidently wrong answers rather than an error. Always write FALSE, or 0, unless you specifically want banding behaviour.

questions.question: EmpID is in A2. Return the name from the Emp table, with "Not found" when there is no match. Use XLOOKUP.
questions.explanation: XLOOKUP takes the not-found message as its fourth argument, so no IFERROR wrapper is needed. It also defaults to exact match and can look leftward - the three things that make VLOOKUP awkward.

questions.question: Why does INDEX + MATCH survive a column being inserted when VLOOKUP does not?
options: MATCH finds the column by its header each time, instead of a fixed number
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP's column index is a hard-coded number, so inserting a column shifts the data without changing the 3. INDEX + MATCH asks where the column is, every time - the lookup repairs itself.

questions.question: Your company is on Excel 2016, which has no XLOOKUP. You need a leftward lookup. What do you use?
options: VLOOKUP with a negative column number
Rearrange the source data so the key is on the left
questions.explanation: INDEX + MATCH has no direction restriction and works in every version. Rearranging someone else's source data is the option that breaks whatever else depends on it - avoid it when a formula will do.

questions.question: Approximate match requires the lookup column to be sorted ascending.
questions.explanation: On unsorted data it returns whatever it happens to land on, with no error. That is precisely why approximate match is the right tool for banded tables - tax slabs, grades, discount tiers - where the bands are naturally in order.

questions.question: In a banded table starting 0, 7, 21, 90, an approximate-match lookup of 11.4 returns the band for which value?
questions.explanation: Approximate match finds the largest value not exceeding the lookup, so 11.4 falls in the 7 band. Each row's number is the floor of its band, which is why the first band must start at the lowest possible value.

questions.question: A VLOOKUP works on 400 rows and returns #N/A on 30. The IDs look identical. What is the most likely cause?
options: The table range is not locked with $
The 30 are text where the others are numbers, or carry trailing spaces
questions.explanation: A lookup compares types as well as characters, so the text "1001" never matches the number 1001. Check with ISNUMBER on both sides, and remember TRIM for the space case.

questions.question: What makes INDIRECT risky in a shared workbook?
options: It builds a reference from text, so renaming a sheet silently breaks it
questions.explanation: Excel updates real references when you rename a sheet, but INDIRECT's reference is just a string, so it becomes #REF! and nothing warned you. Use it only where a dynamic reference is genuinely needed.

questions.question: Write an INDEX + MATCH that finds the value in C2:C100 for the ID in F2, where IDs are in A2:A100.
questions.explanation: MATCH returns the position; INDEX returns what sits at that position. The 0 forces exact match, and it is as easy to forget here as in VLOOKUP - without it MATCH assumes sorted data.

questions.question: What does `=CHOOSE(2,"North","South","East")` return?
questions.explanation: CHOOSE picks the nth item from a list written into the formula. It suits a short fixed list - quarters, a status map - but a list that changes belongs in cells, not inside a formula.

questions.question: XLOOKUP can return several adjacent columns at once.
questions.explanation: Give it a multi-column return array and it spills the whole row - name, department and location from one formula. That replaces three separate lookups and keeps them in step.

questions.question: Someone asks why your lookups use whole-column references like A:A and whether that is a problem.
options: On large workbooks it forces far more cells to be evaluated, so a bounded range or a Table reference is better
It is fine and always fastest
Whole columns do not work in lookups
questions.explanation: Whole-column references are convenient and cost calculation time on large files. A Table reference gives you the convenience without the cost, because it expands to exactly the rows in use.

questions.question: A two-way lookup needs a value at the intersection of a row and a column. Which combination does it?
options: INDEX with MATCH for the row and MATCH for the column
questions.explanation: INDEX takes a row number and a column number, so one MATCH supplies each. It is the cleanest two-way lookup and does not care whether either axis is sorted.

questions.question: When you fill a VLOOKUP down a column, Excel keeps the table range fixed for you.
questions.explanation: It does not - you must lock it with $ yourself. Without locking, the range drifts down with each row and the last formulas search a range that no longer covers the data - returning #N/A at the bottom while the top looks fine. A Table reference avoids the issue entirely.
